title: Regional test-negative vaccine study: a partly unsupported decision refused, scoping review accepted, a cited record's year corrected on the Design route
notes: Adversarial path on a clear scoping-review question (routing scoping-review, explicit under both classifier rules): a regional agency maps methods choices in test-negative influenza vaccine effectiveness studies before writing its own protocol. A fixture search returns eight records (one undated, kept null); the appraisal records five claims whose passages and numbers occur in the cited abstracts. The first design reply cites c2 and 'c9'; c9 is not in the ledger and carries the decision's main assertion. It is dropped with an issue, and the partly supported decision must stay blocked and its acceptance be refused, because the dropped id remains a blocker (S1, S8; WO D13 change to test #35) although the remaining claim and the met gates would let it through at 875fe59. The revised reply supersedes it (withdrawn, kept) and rests on c1, c2 and c4; its acceptance is a supported positive (accepted, ready). After protocol and analysis, the investigator opens Design from the stage list; there the provider corrects the publication year of the rapid antigen record cited by c2 from 2024 to 2014, which takes the only support for criterion k2 (test type became live since 2020) out of that period: the decision must become stale and blocked in the store, on screen, after reload and in the export, with completed stages flagged. The record keeps its DOI-based id. Record ids were computed by a generator script that loads stableRecordId from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59: normalised-DOI hash for records 1, 3, 4, 5, 8 (ev-1z0pzrl, ev-0bf6hlb, ev-1bsnsg0, ev-001qucq, ev-0t8a94f) and titleYearKey hash for records 2, 6, 7 (ev-1vhpb5t, ev-1p35st2, ev-0kurypy). Requires S1 and S8 (refusal of a partly unsupported decision), S10 (revision covers the metadata a claim depends on), S11, S13 and D5. Catches: partial support treated as support, a superseded decision erased, and an accepted decision left current after a cited record's date moves out of the period it was cited for.

inputs.need:
I am an epidemiologist in a regional public health agency. Every winter we are asked how well the seasonal influenza vaccine is working in our region, and we plan to run our own test-negative design study from the 2027 to 2028 season, using patients tested for influenza in our sentinel general practices and hospital laboratories. Before we write a protocol, I would like to do a scoping review of how published test-negative influenza vaccine effectiveness studies have made their key methods choices, because the published estimates vary widely and I suspect that methods explain much of it.

The choices I care about are the clinical case definition used to decide who is tested, the laboratory test (PCR or rapid antigen), how long after symptom onset specimens were taken, how calendar time within the season was handled, whether patients tested more than once were excluded, how prior-season vaccination was measured, and, since 2020, whether patients positive for SARS-CoV-2 were kept as controls. I also want to know how studies have taken vaccination status from immunisation registers rather than self-report, and whether any have reported results separately for older adults in care homes.

I need help with the scope, the search, how to chart methods choices consistently, and how to present the map so that it informs our protocol without pretending to estimate effectiveness. I have a public health registrar for three months and access to the agency library.
inputs.constraints: One public health registrar for three months from January 2027; agency library access only; no contact with study authors beyond one email each; the map must be ready before the protocol is written in May 2027.

The agency library agreed to run the database searches and provide 20 hours of support (request ALIB-2026-58).
A second reviewer from the regional university has agreed to double-screen 20 percent of records.

records.title: Assumptions and biases of the test-negative design for influenza vaccine effectiveness: a methods overview
records.authors: Lindqvist-Obuya H, Moreau-Santos C, Tanaka-Pearce D
records.abstract: We describe the assumptions under which the test-negative design gives unbiased estimates of influenza vaccine effectiveness. The key assumptions are that vaccination does not change the risk of illness from other causes, that vaccinated and unvaccinated patients seek care alike, and that testing does not depend on vaccination status. Biases arise from broad or inconsistent case definitions, late specimen collection, inclusion of repeat tests from the same patient and poor adjustment for calendar time. We recommend that studies report each of these choices explicitly.

records.title: Methods reporting in 112 test-negative influenza vaccine effectiveness studies: a systematic survey
records.abstract: We systematically surveyed 112 test-negative studies of seasonal influenza vaccine effectiveness published between 2010 and 2018. Only 38 of 112 studies restricted testing to patients meeting a clinical case definition. In all, 44 percent adjusted for calendar time at intervals finer than a month, and specimen timing after symptom onset was reported in 61 percent. Prior-season vaccination was measured in 27 percent. Reporting was most complete in studies from established sentinel networks. The authors propose a minimum reporting list for future studies.

records.title: Repeated testing and prior-season vaccination in test-negative studies: a simulation study
records.abstract: We simulated test-negative studies under realistic testing patterns to examine two common choices. Including repeat tests from the same patient biased estimates towards the null by up to 8 percentage points when testing was frequent among vaccinated patients. Ignoring prior-season vaccination distorted estimates when repeated vaccination changed the protection given by the current vaccine. Restricting to the first test per patient per season removed most of the bias from repeat testing. The simulations assumed accurate laboratory tests. The authors recommend that every study report both choices explicitly.

records.title: SARS-CoV-2-positive controls in test-negative influenza vaccine effectiveness studies after 2020: a methodological review
records.authors: Harrington-Adeyemi S, Kowalczyk-Moyo R, Ito-Brennan F
records.abstract: We reviewed test-negative influenza vaccine effectiveness studies published since 2021 for how they handled patients who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2. Of 46 studies published since 2021, 29 excluded SARS-CoV-2-positive patients from the control group, 11 kept them and 6 did not report the choice. Keeping them as controls can bias estimates when COVID-19 vaccination is correlated with influenza vaccination. Few studies reported sensitivity analyses for this choice. Studies that kept SARS-CoV-2-positive controls came more often from settings with high COVID-19 vaccine uptake. The authors recommend reporting results both with and without them.

records.title: Rapid antigen versus PCR testing and outcome misclassification in test-negative influenza studies
records.abstract: We compared rapid antigen tests with PCR in 2,860 patients with influenza-like illness who were tested with both methods in sentinel practices. In all, 21 percent of rapid-antigen-negative patients were PCR-positive, so rapid testing would place many true cases among the controls. In a simulated test-negative analysis, relying on rapid antigen results alone lowered vaccine effectiveness estimates by 9 percentage points. Misclassification was greatest early in the illness. The authors recommend confirming negative rapid tests by PCR in effectiveness studies.

records.title: Register-based versus self-reported vaccination status in test-negative studies of older adults
records.abstract: We compared self-reported influenza vaccination with the immunisation register for 1,530 adults aged 65 or over enrolled in a test-negative study. Self-report agreed with the register for 86 percent of participants. Disagreement was more common among people with cognitive impairment and among those vaccinated in pharmacies, whose vaccinations were sometimes missing from the register. Effectiveness estimates differed by 5 percentage points depending on the source used. The authors recommend linking to registers where possible and checking pharmacy records for people vaccinated outside general practice.

records.title: Test-negative studies in care home residents: a scoping note on methods and gaps
records.abstract: This technical note summarises how test-negative studies have included residents of care homes. It finds that residents are often excluded because testing practices differ from those in the community, that outbreak testing breaks the assumption that testing does not depend on vaccination status, and that very few studies report results for residents separately. The note gives no publication date and does not describe how studies were found. It recommends separate analyses for residents where numbers allow. Residents were included in fewer than one in ten of the studies it describes.

records.title: Time since symptom onset and influenza vaccine effectiveness estimates: a pooled analysis of five seasons
records.authors: Nyberg-Oduya K, Farrell-Tanaka S, Lopez-Achebe M
records.abstract: We pooled five seasons of sentinel test-negative data to examine specimen timing. Estimates were 12 percentage points lower when specimens collected more than 7 days after symptom onset were included, because viral shedding declines and late cases are misclassified as negatives. Restricting to specimens taken within 4 days of onset gave the most stable estimates across seasons. Timing was missing for 9 percent of specimens. The authors recommend that studies report specimen timing and restrict or stratify by it. The effect of timing was similar across age groups.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Methods overviews and a survey of 112 studies show that test-negative studies vary widely in case definition, calendar-time adjustment, specimen timing and prior vaccination, and often do not report these choices. Simulations and pooled analyses show that repeat tests, late specimens and rapid antigen testing each move estimates by several percentage points. Since 2021 studies have handled SARS-CoV-2-positive controls inconsistently. Care home residents are rarely reported separately. The evidence supports mapping methods choices rather than pooling estimates.
response.gradeRationale: Methods overviews, simulations and observational or meta-research studies; consistent in showing variation but indirect for any single choice.
response.summary: Eight retrieved records appraised; five claims; overall certainty low.

steps.note: Appraisal of the eight retrieved records (S13); certainty low (G1).

response.reading: Each methods choice acts on one assumption of the test-negative design: case definitions and specimen timing on who counts as a case, test type on misclassification, repeat testing and calendar time on comparability, prior vaccination on what effectiveness means, and SARS-CoV-2-positive controls on whether controls represent the vaccinated population. The literature varies on every choice, so the map is the evidence the protocol needs.
